blocks.html: WhatsApp Business API for healthcare lets hospitals, clinics and diagnostic labs send appointment reminders, confirmations and follow-ups on the app patients already use, but the rules are stricter than in most industries. The opportunity is real: fewer phone calls for your front desk and fewer forgotten slots. The risk is real too: health information needs careful handling.

This guide explains what hospitals and clinics in India use the WhatsApp API for, the policy that limits health information, how template categories work, template structures you can adapt, consent, integration with your booking system, SMS and voice fallback, and how to budget. sections.heading: What Hospitals and Clinics Use the WhatsApp API For

blocks.html: Most healthcare use cases are administrative, and they remove a lot of manual work. Start with the one that costs your front desk the most time.

items.desc: send a confirmation when a slot is booked and reminders before the visit. Your booking system can trigger them by API or webhook.

items.title: Report-ready alerts:
items.desc: tell patients a report is ready, with a link to a secure portal and no results in the message.

items.title: Billing notices:
items.desc: send pending-bill reminders with a secure payment link.

items.title: Post-visit follow-ups:
items.desc: check in after a visit, and invite feedback.

sections.heading: The Rule That Matters Most: Health Information on WhatsApp

blocks.html: WhatsApp's own Business Messaging Policy sets the limit. It says not to use WhatsApp for telemedicine, or to send or request any health-related information, if applicable regulations prohibit sending that information to systems that do not meet heightened requirements for health data. Read the WhatsApp Business Messaging Policy yourself, and check what applies to you.

items.title: Keep clinical details out:
items.desc: no diagnoses, test results, prescriptions or conditions in a message or a template variable.

items.title: Use a secure portal:
items.desc: for reports and records, send a short alert and link to a login-protected page.

items.title: No telemedicine on WhatsApp:
items.desc: use a dedicated telehealth system for consultations.

items.title: Minimise personal data:
items.desc: send only what the message needs, such as the date, time and clinic.

items.title: DPDP Act:
items.desc: treat patient details as personal data, collected for a clear purpose and kept only as long as needed.

blocks.html: This is practical guidance rather than legal advice, so check your own obligations with a qualified professional.

sections.heading: Template Categories for Healthcare: Utility vs Marketing

blocks.html: To message patients first, you need approved templates, and the category you choose decides how they are reviewed and billed. Keep each template to one purpose.

items.title: Utility:
items.desc: informational messages that follow something the patient did, such as appointment confirmations and reminders, report-ready notices and bill reminders.

items.title: Marketing:
items.desc: promotions and invitations, such as health camps, package offers and seasonal campaigns. These need their own template and an opt-out.

items.title: Authentication:
items.desc: OTPs for patient-portal login. See WhatsApp OTP vs SMS OTP.

items.title: Do not mix them:
items.desc: a reminder that also promotes a package can be reclassified as marketing, which changes review and billing.

sections.heading: Healthcare Template Structures You Can Adapt

blocks.html: Write each template for one purpose, with clear variables and no clinical detail. The examples below use Meta's numbered variable style, such as {{1}}. They are structures to adapt, and they must be approved by Meta before use.

items.title: Appointment confirmed (utility):
items.desc: "Hello {{1}}, your appointment with {{2}} at [Hospital] is confirmed for {{3}}. To change it, tap Reschedule."

items.title: Reminder (utility):
items.desc: "Reminder from [Hospital]: your appointment is on {{1}} at {{2}}. Please confirm or reschedule." Add Confirm and Reschedule buttons.

items.title: Report ready (utility):
items.desc: "Hello {{1}}, your report from [Hospital] is ready. View it securely here: {{2}}" The link opens a login-protected page.

items.title: Pending bill (utility):
items.desc: "Hello {{1}}, your bill for your visit on {{2}} is pending. Pay securely here: {{3}}"

items.title: Health camp invitation (marketing):
items.desc: "[Hospital] is holding a health camp on {{1}} at {{2}}. Reply YES to register, or STOP to opt out."

items.q: Can hospitals and clinics use the WhatsApp Business API in India?
items.a: Yes, for non-clinical patient communication such as appointment confirmations, reminders, billing notices and follow-ups, through the WhatsApp Business Platform with approved templates and patient opt-in. WhatsApp's policy limits health information, so keep clinical details out of your messages and check your own regulatory obligations.

items.q: Are appointment reminders utility or marketing templates?
items.a: Appointment confirmations and reminders are generally utility templates, because they follow something the patient already did. Utility templates must stay informational. If a reminder also promotes a package or offer, Meta can reclassify it as marketing, which changes how it is reviewed and billed. Keep each template to one purpose.

items.q: Can I send lab reports on WhatsApp?
items.a: Sending reports as attachments is risky, because WhatsApp's policy says not to send or request health-related information where regulations require stricter handling than WhatsApp provides. A safer approach is a short "report ready" message with a link to a secure, login-protected portal, with no results or diagnosis in the message itself.

items.q: Do clinics need patient consent for WhatsApp messages?
items.a: Yes. Meta's policy requires opt-in, and the DPDP Act points the same way with clear consent, a stated purpose and easy withdrawal. Collect consent at registration or booking, say which message types patients will receive, keep a record, and honour opt-outs. This is practical guidance rather than legal advice.

items.q: Can WhatsApp be used for telemedicine?
items.a: WhatsApp's policy says not to use it for telemedicine or to send or request health information where applicable regulations prohibit distributing it to systems that do not meet heightened requirements. Use a dedicated telehealth system for consultations, and use WhatsApp for scheduling, reminders and non-clinical updates.

items.q: Is the WhatsApp Business API different from the WhatsApp Business app for clinics?
items.a: Yes. The app suits very small clinics chatting from a phone. The API connects to your booking or hospital system, sends approved templates automatically, supports a shared inbox for several staff and keeps records in your own systems. Our guide on the WhatsApp Business app vs the API covers the difference.

items.q: Does WhatsApp messaging for patients need DLT registration?
items.a: No. DLT registration under TRAI's rules applies to SMS. WhatsApp follows Meta's template approval and opt-in policies. If you add an SMS fallback for patients who are not on WhatsApp, that SMS still needs your DLT entity, sender ID and approved template.

items.q: How much does the WhatsApp API cost for a hospital?
items.a: Meta bills per delivered template message, by category and the recipient's country, and utility and marketing templates are billed differently. Check Meta's official pricing page for current rates, and ask any provider for an itemised quote that separates Meta's charges from platform fees and says whether GST is included.
